title: Shalom Aleichem
hookLine: the Friday night song welcomes angels; the Talmud says two walk you home (Shabbat 119b)
tomorrow: a guest at the Friday table

lines: THE WALK HOME ON FRIDAY NIGHT.
A SONG FOR GUESTS NO ONE CAN SEE.
cards: Friday night, the walk home from synagogue. The streets are quieter than usual. Somebody has a child on their shoulders.
Maybe it's cold, maybe it's warm and you can hear other families' dinners through open windows. You open your door: the candles are already burning, the table is set.
And before anyone sits down, the family stands around the table and starts to sing. Not to each other. To guests nobody can see.

teach.b: Shalom aleichem means peace be upon you. It's also an everyday greeting, a hello in Hebrew and Yiddish. But on Friday night it's a song, sung to angels.
The idea comes from a story in the Talmud.
Two ministering angels, it says, walk a person home from synagogue on Friday night, one good and one bad.

teach.h: MAY IT BE LIKE THIS NEXT TIME.
teach.b: If the candles are lit, the table is set and the beds are made, the good angel says: may it be like this next Shabbat too. And the bad angel has no choice but to answer amen.

If the house is dark and nothing's ready, it goes the other way around, and the good angel has to say amen. It's a story about habit: the way you welcome this week shapes the next. The song is much younger than the story.
Tradition traces it to Kabbalist circles, many centuries after the Talmud. It has four short verses, often each sung three times.

teach.h: WELCOME, COME, BLESS, GO IN PEACE.
teach.b: Welcome, angels of peace. Come in peace. Bless me with peace.
Go in peace. Some people ask, reasonably, why you'd tell angels to leave. One answer is simple courtesy: they walked you home, and now you can let them go.
Another is that the family is about to sit down together, and some moments are just for the people at the table. Families sing it to many tunes, fast and slow. Some hold hands.
Some sing it once, quietly, alone.

teach.h: THE DOORWAY WHERE PEACE COMES IN.
teach.b: It turns an ordinary doorway into the place where the week's peace comes in.

how: On Friday night, after returning from synagogue and before Kiddush, many families stand around the table and sing Shalom Aleichem, each of its four verses three times.

o: a lullaby sung to babies at bedtime each night
a toast made to the guest of honor at a party
peace be upon you, sung to angels on Friday night

games.q: what's inside the song — tap the pairs.
p: may it be like this next Shabbat

s: the song Shalom Aleichem is written in the Talmud
the Talmud tells the story of the two angels; the song came much later, from the Kabbalists.
in the story, one of the angels is bad
one good, one bad; if the house is ready, the bad one has to say amen.
shalom aleichem is also an everyday greeting
it's a common hello: peace be upon you.

games.q: you're the bad angel in the Talmud's story. you arrive at a home where the candles are lit, the table set, the beds made. the good angel says: may it be like this next Shabbat. what do you say?
o: may it be dark next time.
games.why: the bad angel has no choice but to answer amen: the way you welcome this week shapes the next.

practice: Picture the next door you'll walk through, home, work, a friend's place, and your hand on it. Pick any tune that feels like peace to you and hum a little of it, even under your breath.
Picture walking through that door humming, with two quiet companions beside you, noticing what kind of place you've made.

wordCard.voice: Shalom Aleichem. Peace be upon you: a greeting, and the Friday night song that welcomes the angels of peace home.

orig.note: Hebrew: peace be upon you. the answer is aleichem shalom, upon you be peace.

carryVoice: Your line: angels walk you home. Come in peace, go in peace. That's day one hundred.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Shabbat 119b (two angels walk a person home)
